title: New York: laundry job, Jack Pettis and Irving Mills record dates
summary: He tells of work in New York, joining Jack Pettis, record dates and a mellophone session behind Ethel Waters.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I made a bunch of them in New York. Now, I went to, when I, I went to work New York, I first went to work in a, a laundry. You know these Chinese, they used to call them laundries. Well I worked in the laundry for about six, seven months. And then I went to work with a fella by the name of Jack Pettis, who originally played with the Rhythm Kings. And then went with Ben Burnie. Well after he left Ben Burnie, he made up his own band. So I went to work with him. Perini was in the band. And this boy that committed suicide, the, Donnie Pottle, bass player, he's, he's from here. He's Ralph Pottle's brother. He jumped off the bridge there. He was in the band. And, uh, Charlie Butterfield, he did, makes a lot of these network programs. You know the brothers, they're from, yeah. And, uh, who else was in, somebody else was in the band from New Orleans. It was a big band. Well we, we, we were working for Irving Mills. Irving Mills at that time controlled every record date in New York. And he controlled all the vaudeville. And the, the bands. He controlled all, all of that, you see. Well I went to work with Pettis. And, uh, we used to make, Bill, we used to make us five or six record dates a week. We, the, there was only the big four then. And then they had this one place way downtown in New York. They used to make all of these little labels. Perfect, Black Swan, O'Reo, oh they must, they must have had 50 labels. Yeah. They were all made at this one place. Then you had, you had O.K., Columbia, Brunswick, and Victor. Well Victor used to make everything, he didn't make anything in New York. He used to make everything at Camden. And, uh, well we made for those, for the big four. And then we used to make a bunch of them for the, so Irving Mills took a light in him. He heard me playing. And I used to scat sing in those days. He went, that's what he really went for. He went for the scat singing. And, uh, he take and put me in, like I told you, he controlled it. He had Ellington at the time. He had Callaway. He had the Mills Blue Ribbon. He had some kind of Sweethearts, a girls band, big colored girls band. He had every big jig band in the country, he had them all tied up. He was like Gabler. And, uh, he put me with these different bands, like we, we, we, uh, we did a date. We were making a record and, uh, there's a fella by the name of Goof Moyer that used to play mellophone and saxophone. I don't know whether you ever heard of it. Well, uh, they had hired Goof to play mellophone on this record date. See, but Goof didn't play any of them. See, but Goof didn't play anything but straight. He just played the straight lead, you see. So after we made one, one, one test, uh, Pat Astorin said, no, he says, I want you to take off. See, so, man, we played again. God did the same thing. He played the lead right straight through again, you see. So Jack says, hey Mark, where's your mellophone? I said, it's at the house. I think we were on Fifth Avenue around, around 49th, 50th Street, somewhere around this way. I think we were at Victor. We were at Victor, because I know, I can associate this with it. So he said, uh, go home and get your mellophone. So he went out to whoever the guy that had the record for the day, they told him, I said, man, I got a drummer who played more mellophone than that guy. So I went home and I got the mellophone and I wound up making the date. So while we were making the date, who comes in the studio but Red Allen and a couple other jigs, and they were making, they were making a record with Ethel Waters. She sang blues in those days. That's about the time she sang all those things, get up off your knees, you know, and all those. Yeah. And, uh, they come in there, they heard, they were, Red said, as soon as I heard the beat, I knew there had to be somebody from down home, you know. So they come in there, so I wound up going with the mellophone, leaving, finishing up our date, and then going over there and making, making the, making the date behind, behind Ethel Waters with them.
